summary: Describes an architecture for handing out IPv6 unicast addresses across the Internet. The goal is to structure allocation hierarchically so routes can be aggregated and routing tables stay manageable. It is informational and does not define a standard.

eli5.summary: Imagine giving out street addresses so that all houses in a town share the same start. Then mail trucks only need to know the town, not every single house.

questions: how are ipv6 addresses allocated hierarchically
subtitle: How to divide the IPv6 address space among Internet providers and sites to keep routing efficient.

tldr.problem: IPv6 will eventually serve hundreds of thousands of routing domains. If addresses are assigned randomly, each router must maintain a separate routing entry for every domain. This does not scale; the routing tables would become unmanageable.
tldr.mechanism: Assign IPv6 addresses hierarchically, grouped by network topology: providers get prefixes, then allocate parts of their prefix to sites beneath them. A router then only needs one entry per provider, not one per site. The hierarchy can extend through several levels (continental, national, provider, site) to achieve maximum aggregation.
tldr.outcome: This architecture became the foundation for IPv6 address allocation. Hierarchical addressing is now standard practice and enables global routing to scale to billions of devices.

today: RFC 1887 is Informational. Its architectural principles became fundamental to IPv6 deployment. Hierarchical, provider-based address allocation remains the standard approach, enabling global routing to scale across billions of connected devices.

sections.title: Scope and Goals
sections.content:
This RFC defines an architecture for allocating IPv6 unicast addresses across the Internet. It focuses on the technical aspects of allocation, not administrative procedures. The goal is to enable address assignment in a way that supports efficient routing.

The Internet is modeled as domains under different administrative authorities. Network service providers (NSPs) control backbone and regional networks. Subscribers are individual organizations, campuses, or corporations that connect to one or more providers. The architecture must accommodate this hierarchical structure while allowing efficient information abstraction at routing domain boundaries.
sections.eli5: The plan is to give addresses so that routers can group traffic by provider, not by individual company.

sections.title: Routing and Hierarchical Addresses
sections.content:
IPv6 partitions the routing problem into three parts: end systems to routers, routers within a domain, and routing among domains. The key insight is that if all hosts within a routing domain are assigned addresses from a single prefix, the domain can announce itself to other domains using just that one prefix. The domain's internal structure becomes invisible to the wider internet.

The RFC distinguishes between topological and administrative boundaries. A coherent addressing plan must balance the need for administrative independence with the need for addresses to reflect network topology, so that address prefixes can be aggregated in the routing system.
sections.eli5: When all the houses in a town start with the same number, mail trucks only look at that number, not the street address. That keeps mail systems simple.

sections.title: Hierarchical Allocation Structure
sections.content:
The recommended structure has several levels. At the top, a continental prefix (such as 46/8 for Europe) is assigned to a continent. Within a continent, national backbones and regional providers receive address blocks derived from the continental prefix. Each provider then allocates parts of its block to the leaf routing domains (sites) it serves.

This layering allows aggregation at each level: a backbone seeing routes from many providers can summarize them all as one continental prefix when announcing to other continents. The greatest gains come at the lowest levels (leaf domains), where the number of entities grows exponentially.

The RFC notes that diminishing returns eventually set in; beyond a certain point, adding more levels of hierarchy provides little benefit because the number of providers at high levels remains small enough to handle directly.
sections.eli5: Continental prefix covers whole continents; providers under that prefix cover countries; sites under each provider cover local companies. Each level only needs to know what is directly below it.

sections.title: Single-Homed and Multi-Homed Domains
sections.content:
Most sites attach to the Internet through a single provider. These single-homed domains are straightforward: they receive a prefix from their provider and use that prefix for all their hosts. This arrangement allows the provider to aggregate the site's prefix with others into its own announcement.

Some large organizations attach to multiple providers (multi-homed). For these domains, the RFC presents four possible solutions, each with different trade-offs. Solution 1 assigns a global prefix independent of any provider; other providers must then maintain explicit routes to it. Solution 2 assigns a separate prefix per provider connection; traffic enters via the nearest provider. Solutions 3 and 4 represent intermediate approaches for special cases.

The RFC also covers zero-homed domains (private networks with no global connectivity) and private address spaces for hosts that never need to leave their organization.
sections.eli5: Most companies get an address from one provider and use just that. Big companies attached to many providers have to pick an approach: one global address (simple, but everyone remembers it), or separate addresses per provider (efficient, but must change addresses if they drop a provider).

sections.title: Recommendations for Address Allocation
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that the great majority of sites obtain prefixes from their provider's address space. This maximizes aggregation benefit. It further recommends that providers within a continent obtain their addresses from the continental prefix, enabling continental-level aggregation when routes cross oceans.

For sites connected to multiple TRDs, the RFC acknowledges that no single solution fits all cases. Economic and technical considerations will require a variety of approaches, with site and provider policies balanced against global routing efficiency.

The RFC emphasizes that address allocation must be consistent with actual network topology, not organizational boundaries. Administrative decentralization is important, but assigning addresses along non-topological lines (such as arbitrary organizational units) defeats the goals of the architecture.
sections.eli5: Companies should get addresses from their provider. Providers on one continent should get their addresses from that continent's pool. But some special cases need special rules.

sections.title: Limitations and Open Questions
sections.content:
The RFC does not address several topics: specific address assignment plans, embedding IPv4 addresses within IPv6, multicast addressing, mobility, policy routing details, how sites should organize internal topology, or procedures for assigning addresses to individual hosts within a domain.

The architecture also does not mandate a single solution for all multi-homed scenarios; real-world deployment will require negotiation between organizations and service providers. The document serves as a framework and set of principles, not a detailed operational specification.
sections.eli5: The plan covers the big picture—who gets which chunks of addresses—but leaves many details to be worked out case by case.
